content.rendered:
Written by Sonny Bono and Jack Nitzsche, “Needles and Pins” was first recorded in 1963 by Jackie DeShannon, who scored a minor hit with it, peaking at #84 in the U.S. (but taking it all the way to the top in Canada.)

But it was most likely The Searchers’ version the following year that brought the song to Bruce’s attention. Their cover was an international hit, reaching #13 in the U.S. but cracking the top ten in Germany, Sweden, and Norway and reaching the top spot in the U.K, Ireland, and South Africa.

Regardless of whose version captured Bruce’s imagination, he was definitely taken with the song. Over the course of the Born to Run Tour, Bruce soundchecked “Needles and Pins” three different times that we know of–in February, July, and December.

Given how rare it is for us to have a setlist (much less a recording) of a soundcheck from that era, it’s likely that Bruce rehearsed it regularly throughout 1975.

Why didn’t he actually play it during a show? I have no idea. But we’re fortunate to at least have one recording (albeit a muffled one) of Bruce playing this early rock classic. Take a listen to Bruce playing “Needles and Pins” at his soundcheck in Geneva, New York, on July 22, 1975.

Bonus: here’s a clearer recording from a soundcheck earlier in the year: February 23rd at the Westbury Music Fair. Unfortunately, we only have thirty seconds of it, but it’s a nice listen anyway.

Needles and Pins
Never performed in concert
First soundchecked: February 23, 1975 (Westbury, NY)
Last soundchecked: December 12, 1975 (Greenvale, NY)

© February 27, 2019

excerpt.rendered: Never performed but occasionally soundchecked, Bruce was clearly taken with The Searchers’ “Needles and Pins” during the Born to Run tour.

jetpack-related-posts.title: When You Walk in the Room
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Bruce debuted his cover of "When You Walk in the Room" at his legendary stand at the Bottom Line; he reprised it more than thirty years later.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cover Me: Any Other Way
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Even Bruce Springsteen's musical encyclopedia can miss an entry or two, as evidenced by his adaptation of this William Bell song transformed by Jackie Shane.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cover Me, Dave Alvin: Seeds
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: As far as I'm concerned, Dave Alvin's cover of "Seeds" is the definitive version of the song.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cover Me, Richie Havens: Streets of Philadelphia
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: An unfortunate licensing snafu resulted in one of the finest covers of a Springsteen song.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Ring of Fire
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Traditional, slow-grooving, or hard-rocking, they're all great: check out Bruce's three very different covers of Johnny Cash's "Ring of Fire" spanning five decades.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Roll of the Dice: Drive Fast (The Stuntman)
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: My favorite song on Western Stars is arguably the most romantic and (literally) cinematic song in Bruce's entire catalog.
